question: What was the procedural history in the case where part-time sweepers of a State school education department, appointed on various dates between 1987 and 2001, obtained a Madras High Court direction to regularise their services on a full-time basis with time scale of pay after completing ten years?
answer: The part-time sweepers, appointed between 1.12.1987 and 19.1.2001, filed writ petitions in 2012 which the Madras High Court allowed on 23.7.2012 with a direction to regularise their services on a full-time basis with time scale of pay from completion of 10 years of service; the State's writ appeals were dismissed, leading to the appeals before the Supreme Court.
gold_passage:
The respondents had been appointed as part-time sweepers by appellant from 1987
till 1993 as their initial appointments had been issued to the respondents and others
on 1.12.1987, 2.5.1991, 1.4.1993, 10.4.1993, 27.5.1999 and 19.1.2001. As the
respondents and others had been working for more than 10 years, they filed Writ
Petition Nos.
17468, 17470, 17472, 17473, 17469 and 17471 of 2012 before the High Court of Madras for seeking
regularisation of their services. The said Writ Petitions were allowed by the common judgment and
order dated 23.7.2012 with the direction to regularise the services of the respondents on full time
basis based on the individual representation after verifying their service particulars from the date of
completion of 10 years of service with time scale of pay.
Aggrieved, the appellant preferred the writ appeals which were dismissed.
Hence, these appeals.

question: In the challenge to a Central Government order under Section 396 of the Companies Act, 1956 compulsorily amalgamating a national spot commodities exchange with its parent technology company, what did the Department of Consumer Affairs direct the exchange to do on 12.07.2013 without adjudicating the pending show cause notice regarding violation of its FCRA exemption?
answer: Without adjudicating the show cause notice, the DCA on 12.07.2013 directed NSEL to give an undertaking that no further contracts would be launched until further instructions and that all existing contracts would be settled on due dates - effectively a freezing order; NSEL gave the undertaking on 22.07.2013.
gold_passage:
NSEL commenced operations in October 2008. On 27.04.2012, the Department of Consumer
Affairs [“DCA”] issued a show cause notice to NSEL as to why action should not be initiated against
it for permitting transactions in alleged violation of the exemption granted to it under the FCRA.
NSEL replied to the show cause notice on 29.05.2012 stating that it had not violated the exemption
granted to it. Without adjudicating upon the show cause notice, on 12.07.2013, the DCA directed
NSEL to give an undertaking that no further contracts shall be launched until further instructions,
and that all existing contracts will be settled on due dates. This was effectively a “freezing” order. On
22.07.2013, NSEL gave an undertaking to the DCA.

question: Did the Supreme Court uphold the appointment of a minority institution's Principal made by the Director of Education under Section 16-F(4) of the U.P. Intermediate Education Act, 1921 after U.P. Act 26 of 1975 had withdrawn that power, where the selection process had commenced in 1973 before the amendment?
answer: Yes; since the selection proceedings had commenced in 1973 and the amending Act had no retrospective effect on pending proceedings, the Director's appointment made after 18 August 1975 was not illegal - the proceedings had to be continued under the law as it stood at their commencement.
gold_passage:
In the instant case admittedly the proceedings for the
selection had commenced in the year 1973 and after the Deputy Director had disapproved the
recommendations made by the Selection Committee twice the Director acquired the jurisdiction to
make an appointment from amongst the qualified candidates who had applied for the vacancy in
question. At the instance of the appellant himself in the earlier writ petition filed by him the High
Court had directed the Director to exercise that power. Although the Director in the present case
exercised that power subsequent to August 18, 1975 on which date the amendment came into force,
it cannot be said that the selection made by him was illegal since the amending law had no
retrospective effect. It did not have any effect on the proceedings which had commenced prior to
August 18, 1975. Such proceedings had to be continued in accordance with the law as it stood at the
commencement of the said proceedings.

question: Can the Railway Claims Tribunal permit a claimant who lacks the means to pay the fee prescribed under Section 16(2) of the Railway Claims Tribunal Act, 1987 to prosecute his compensation claim as an indigent person by invoking the principle of Order XXXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure?
answer: Yes; the Supreme Court held that nothing in the Act or the Rules precludes the Tribunal from invoking Order XXXIII CPC, that access to justice cannot be denied for inability to pay the prescribed fee, and that the Tribunal should follow the Order XXXIII procedure where the ends of justice so require.
gold_passage:
Since the Claims Tribunal is empowered to regulate its own procedure, there is nothing in
the Act and the Rules which precludes the invocation of Order XXXIII of the Code. A view which
advances the cause of justice must be preferred to the one which defeats it. We are, therefore, of the
opinion that the Tribunal adopted a narrow interpretation of the relevant provisions of the Act in
coming to the conclusion that the Act as well as the Rules did not permit invocation of Order XXXIII
of the Code. The view taken by the Tribunal results in a person not having the means to pay the fee
prescribed for preferring a claim being left without a remedy. Such a view would result in gross
injustice. The Tribunal has the power to lay down its own procedure and as stated earlier Section
18(1) does not preclude it from invoking the provisions of Order XXXIII of the Code if the ends of
justice so require. When an indigent person approaches the Tribunal for compensation for the
wrong done to him, the Tribunal cannot refuse to exercise jurisdiction merely because he does not
have the means to pay the fee. In such a situation we think the ends of justice require that the
Tribunal should follow the procedure laid down in Order XXXIII of the Code to do justice for which
it came to be established.

question: Where some co-heirs of a deceased Muslim owner signed an agreement to sell an inherited house but the two sister co-sharers never joined it, did the Supreme Court hold that specific performance could be decreed against the signing co-sharers to the extent of their 5/6th share while refusing the alternative decree of partition in the same suit?
answer: Yes; the Court held that a co-sharer who agrees to sell joint property is bound to execute the sale deed at least to the extent of his own share even if other co-sharers have not joined, so the decree for specific performance of the 5/6th share was upheld, but the decree for partition and separate possession was premature and was set aside.
gold_passage:
15. Thus we have no hesitation to hold, even where any property is held jointly, and once any party
to the contract has agreed to sell such joint property agreement, then, even if other co-sharer has not
joined at least to the extent of his share, he is bound to execute, the sale deed. However, in the
absence of other co-sharer there could not be any decree of any specified part of the property to be
partitioned and possession given. The decree could only be to the extent of transferring the share of
the Appellants in such property to other such contracting party. In the present case, it is not in
dispute that the Appellants have 5/6 share in the property. So, the Plaintiffs suit for specific
performance to the extent of this 5/6th share was rightly decreed by the High Court which requires
no interference.

question: Where a person confined under the 1974 law against foreign-exchange violations and smuggling complained that the Tamil rendering of the grounds supplied to him spoke of stopping the movement of contraband while the English text spoke of curbing smuggling itself, did the mismatch between the two language texts invalidate his custody?
answer: No; the Supreme Court held the alleged difference between the two versions was not consequential, the detention order and accompanying grounds clearly spelt out why the detenu was detained, and no prejudice was caused, so the challenge failed.
gold_passage:
4. We have considered the matter ourselves. We are also not impressed with this submission. The
alleged difference between the two versions is not consequential. The order of detention and
grounds accompanied clearly spelt out why the detenu was being detained. We are not persuaded to
hold that the two versions are so different as to cause any prejudice to the detenu. We, therefore,
agree with the High Court and dismiss the anneal.

question: In the case where a Section 8 application under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was resisted on the ground of serious fraud by partners of a Tirunelveli hotel run under a 1994 family partnership deed, what act of misappropriation of the firm's funds was alleged against the brother who took over the hotel's administration?
answer: It was alleged that after taking over the administration he failed to deposit the day-to-day collections into the hotel's bank account and fraudulently signed and issued a cheque for Rs.10,00,050 dated 17.06.2010 from the hotel's account in favour of his son without the other partners' knowledge, besides keeping the account books from the other partners.
gold_passage:
On the aforesaid understanding, administration
of the hotel was taken over by the appellant. But he did not adhere to the said understanding and
failed to deposit day to day collection into the bank account as promised. It is also agged that the
appellant, fraudulently, signed and issued a cheque for Rs.10,00,050/- dated 17.06.2010 from the
bank account in the name of 'Hotel Arunagiri' in favour of his son without the knowledge and
consent of the other partners and in this manner, the money was siphoned off and misappropriated
from the common fund. It is further alleged that the appellant kept the hotel account books with
him and did not show it to the respondents for their examination.

question: In upholding the Kerala Luxury Tax on Tobacco (Validation) Act, 1964, did the Supreme Court hold that the validated licence fee on the stocking and vending of tobacco was a luxury tax within the State legislature's competence rather than an excise duty beyond it?
answer: Yes; the Court held the impugned provisions had nothing to do with production or manufacture of tobacco - the levy was sought to be made as a luxury tax, which is within the State legislature's competence, and not as an excise duty, so the validation was permissible.
gold_passage:
(5)(a) Where a topic is not included within the relevant List dealing with the legislative competence
of the State Legislature, Parliament, by making a law cannot attempt to confer such legislative
competence on the State legislatures This principle would, however, have no application where what
is sought to be done is to validate the recovery of licence fee for stocking and vending of tobacco. The
impugned provisions have nothing to do with the production and manufacture of tobacco. The levy
is sought to be made as luxury to which is within the competence of State legislature and not as
excise duty which is beyond the legislative competence of the State legislature. If the levy in question
could be justified under a provision which is within the legislative competent of the State legislature,
the levy shall be held to be validly imposed and cannot be considered to be impermissible.

question: In the case where tobacco dealers of the former Cochin and Travancore areas challenged licence fees for storage of tobacco, what replaced the system of auction sales of A class and B class shops after the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 was extended to the Part B State on April 1, 1950?
answer: After the Finance Act, 1950 extended the Central Excises and Salt Act to the State, the rules were changed by notification dated 3 August 1950 for the Cochin area (and 25 January 1951 for Travancore): the auction system was done away with and graded licence fees were introduced for various classes of licensees.
gold_passage:
After this
provision in the Finance Act, 1950 , the Rules
which were in force on April 1, 1950, were changed
in the Cochin area by a notification dated August
3, 1950, and the system of auction sales of A
Class and Class shops was done away with and
instead graded licence fees were introduced for
various classes of licensees. Similar change was
made for the Travancore area by notification dated
January 25, 1951.

question: Can the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142 of the Constitution, reduce a sentence below the statutory minimum prescribed by the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 on grounds of long lapse of time since the trap, the trivial Rs.200 bribe amount, or the convict's loss of employment?
answer: No; the Court held that where the statute prescribes a minimum sentence, delay in disposal, the quantum of the bribe, and loss of job are not grounds for reduction, and even under Article 142 waiver of the statutorily prescribed minimum sentence is not permissible.
gold_passage:
b) Long delay in disposal of appeal or any other factor may not be a ground for
reduction of sentence, particularly, when the statute prescribes minimum sentence.
In other cases where no such minimum sentence is prescribed, it is open to the Court
to consider the delay and its effect and the ultimate decision.
c) In a case of corruption by public servant, quantum of amount is immaterial.
Ultimately it depends upon the conduct of the delinquent and the proof regarding
demand and acceptance established by the prosecution.
d) Merely because the delinquent lost his job due to conviction under the Act may not
be a mitigating circumstance for reduction of sentence, particularly, when the Statute
prescribes minimum sentence.
e) Though Article 142 of the Constitution gives wider power to this Court, waiver of
certain period as prescribed in the Statute imposing lesser sentence than the
minimum prescribed is not permissible.
